prompt: Why does the section introduce the Gibbs energy after the Helmholtz energy?

choices.text: Most processes run at constant P, not constant V
The Helmholtz energy fails for open systems
choices.why: A works for systems that exchange heat, as long as T and V are constant. G is needed because constant pressure is much easier to work at than constant volume.

choices.text: The Helmholtz energy cannot be defined for gases
choices.why: A ≡ U − TS applies to gases too. The Gibbs energy is introduced because isobaric changes are much easier to deal with than isochoric ones.

choices.text: Constant temperature is hard to keep in a lab
choices.why: G also needs constant T, just as A does. What changes is constant V to constant P, the condition most processes run under.

explanation: A suits isochoric (constant-volume) changes, but it is much easier to work at constant pressure. G ≡ H − TS plays the role of A when P and T are held constant.

prompt: How does the section define the Gibbs energy G?

choices.text: G ≡ H − TS
G ≡ U − TS
choices.why: U − TS is the Helmholtz energy A. The Gibbs energy uses the enthalpy: G ≡ H − TS.

choices.text: G ≡ H + TS
choices.why: The TS term is subtracted: G ≡ H − TS. So a larger entropy lowers G.

choices.text: G ≡ U + PV
choices.why: U + PV is the enthalpy H. G subtracts TS from it: G ≡ H − TS.

explanation: G ≡ H − TS, which can also be written U + PV − TS. It is the constant-pressure partner of the Helmholtz energy, A ≡ U − TS.

prompt: How is the Gibbs energy G related to the Helmholtz energy A?

choices.text: G = A + PV
G = A − PV
choices.why: Since H = U + PV, G = H − TS = U − TS + PV = A + PV. The PV term is added, not subtracted.

choices.text: G = A + TS
choices.why: A + TS is U, the internal energy, not G. Since H = U + PV, G = A + PV.

choices.text: G = A − TS
choices.why: A already contains the −TS term. G = U + PV − TS = A + PV.

explanation: G = H − TS = U + PV − TS. Grouping U − TS as A gives G = A + PV.

prompt: Which inequality tests whether a process is spontaneous when T and P are held constant?

choices.text: dG ≤ 0
dA ≤ 0
choices.why: dA ≤ 0 is the test at constant T and V. At constant T and P, the test uses the Gibbs energy: dG ≤ 0.

choices.text: dS ≥ 0
choices.why: The system's entropy alone decides spontaneity only for an isolated system. At constant T and P, the test is dG ≤ 0.

choices.text: dH ≤ 0
choices.why: Giving off heat is not enough, since entropy matters too. At constant T and P, the test is dG ≤ 0, with G ≡ H − TS.

explanation: At constant T and P, dU − T dS + P dV ≤ 0, which is dG ≤ 0. G decreases in a spontaneous process and is constant at equilibrium.

prompt: A process at constant T and P has ΔG = 0. What does the section conclude?

choices.text: The system is at equilibrium
The process is spontaneous
choices.why: A spontaneous process has ΔG < 0. ΔG = 0 means G has stopped changing, so the system is at equilibrium.

choices.text: The reverse process is spontaneous
choices.why: The reverse process is favored when ΔG > 0. When ΔG = 0, neither direction is favored.

choices.text: ΔH and ΔS are both zero
choices.why: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is zero whenever ΔH = TΔS, even if both are large. ΔG = 0 is the condition for equilibrium.

explanation: At constant T and P, G decreases in a spontaneous process and is constant at equilibrium. So ΔG = 0 marks equilibrium, where neither direction is favored.

prompt: A process at constant T and P has ΔG > 0. According to the section, how can it still be made to occur?

choices.text: By coupling it to a process with negative ΔG
By waiting long enough for it to go on its own
choices.why: A process with ΔG > 0 never goes on its own, however long you wait. It has to be pumped by coupling it to a process with ΔG < 0.

choices.text: It already occurs, since ΔG > 0 means spontaneous
choices.why: The sign is the other way round: a spontaneous process has ΔG < 0. A process with ΔG > 0 must be coupled to one with ΔG < 0.

choices.text: It cannot be made to occur by any means
choices.why: The section says it can be pumped, by coupling it to another process with a negative ΔG. It just won't occur on its own.

explanation: A process with positive ΔG is not spontaneous. It can be driven, or pumped, by coupling it to a process with negative ΔG, which is spontaneous.

prompt: At constant temperature and pressure, which expression does the section give for ΔG between two states?

choices.text: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
ΔG = ΔH + TΔS
choices.why: The entropy term enters with a minus sign, as in G ≡ H − TS. So ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and a positive ΔS lowers ΔG.

choices.text: ΔG = ΔU − TΔS
choices.why: ΔU − TΔS is ΔA, the change in the Helmholtz energy. With the enthalpy in place of U, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

choices.text: ΔG = ΔH − SΔT
choices.why: At constant temperature ΔT = 0, so this would just give ΔH. With T fixed, G ≡ H − TS gives ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

explanation: From G ≡ H − TS at constant T, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A spontaneous process has ΔG < 0, and equilibrium has ΔG = 0.

prompt: An exothermic reaction at constant T and P has ΔH = −50 kJ and TΔS = −60 kJ. Is it spontaneous?

choices.text: No, since ΔG = +10 kJ
Yes, since ΔH is negative
choices.why: A negative ΔH alone does not decide spontaneity at constant T and P. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −50 kJ − (−60 kJ) = +10 kJ, which is positive.

choices.text: Yes, since ΔG = −110 kJ
choices.why: That adds TΔS instead of subtracting it. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −50 kJ + 60 kJ = +10 kJ, so the reaction is not spontaneous.

choices.text: It is at equilibrium, since both terms are negative
choices.why: Equilibrium needs ΔG = 0, which would require ΔH = TΔS. Here ΔG = −50 kJ − (−60 kJ) = +10 kJ, so the reaction is not spontaneous.

explanation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −50 kJ − (−60 kJ) = +10 kJ. The entropy loss outweighs the heat given off, so the reaction is not spontaneous at this temperature, even though it is exothermic.

prompt: Why can the spontaneous direction of a reaction at constant pressure change with temperature?

choices.text: T multiplies ΔS in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
ΔH always changes sign at high temperature
choices.why: The section treats ΔH as nearly constant. The direction can flip because the entropy term, −TΔS, grows with T.

choices.text: G is not a state function at high temperature
choices.why: G is a state function at every temperature. The direction can change because T multiplies ΔS, so −TΔS grows as T rises.

choices.text: The pressure rises whenever T rises
choices.why: Here the pressure is held constant. The flip comes from the T in −TΔS, which can make that term outweigh ΔH.

explanation: In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, the entropy term is multiplied by T. At low T, ΔH dominates; at high T, −TΔS can win, so the sign of ΔG, and the direction, can change.

prompt: A reaction at constant pressure has ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0. At which temperatures is it spontaneous?

choices.text: At all temperatures
Only at low temperatures
choices.why: Both ΔH and −TΔS are negative here. Raising T only makes ΔG more negative, so the reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures.

choices.text: Only at high temperatures
choices.why: ΔH is already negative, so ΔG < 0 even at low T. With ΔS > 0, ΔG stays negative as T rises.

choices.text: At no temperature
choices.why: Giving off heat and gaining entropy both lower ΔG. With ΔH < 0 and −TΔS < 0, ΔG is negative at every temperature.

explanation: ΔH < 0 and −TΔS < 0, so ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative whatever the temperature. Such a reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures.

prompt: A process takes in heat (ΔH > 0) and lowers the entropy (ΔS < 0). At constant T and P, when is it spontaneous?

choices.text: At no temperature
At all temperatures
choices.why: Both ΔH and −TΔS are positive here, so ΔG > 0 at every T. The process is never spontaneous as written.

choices.text: Only at high temperatures
choices.why: Raising T makes −TΔS more positive, since ΔS < 0. ΔG only grows, so the process is never spontaneous.

choices.text: Only at low temperatures
choices.why: Even at low T, ΔG ≈ ΔH > 0. Both terms are positive, so ΔG > 0 at every temperature.

explanation: ΔH > 0 and −TΔS > 0, so ΔG > 0 at every temperature. The process never goes forward on its own; its reverse is spontaneous instead.

prompt: For a reaction with ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0 at constant pressure, how does temperature affect whether it is spontaneous?

choices.text: It is spontaneous only below T = ΔH/ΔS
It is spontaneous only above T = ΔH/ΔS
choices.why: Above that temperature, −TΔS (positive, since ΔS < 0) outweighs ΔH, so ΔG > 0. The reaction is favored at low T, where ΔH dominates.

choices.text: It is spontaneous at all temperatures
choices.why: Because ΔS < 0, the term −TΔS is positive and grows with T. Eventually it outweighs ΔH, so the reaction stops being spontaneous.

choices.text: It is never spontaneous
choices.why: At low T, ΔG ≈ ΔH < 0, so the reaction is spontaneous there. It stops being spontaneous only above T = ΔH/ΔS.

explanation: ΔH < 0 favors the reaction, but −TΔS > 0 opposes it and grows with T. ΔG < 0 below T = ΔH/ΔS and ΔG > 0 above it, as for NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s).

prompt: Below 0 °C water freezes, and above 0 °C ice melts. Melting has ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0. Why does ice melt only above 0 °C?

choices.text: Only then does TΔS exceed ΔH
Only then does ΔH become negative
choices.why: Melting always takes in heat, so ΔH > 0 at every temperature. Above 0 °C the term TΔS becomes larger than ΔH, making ΔG < 0.

choices.text: Only then does ΔS become positive
choices.why: Liquid water has more entropy than ice at the same temperature, so ΔS > 0 throughout. What changes is the size of TΔS compared with ΔH.

choices.text: Only then does ΔG become positive
choices.why: A positive ΔG would mean melting is not spontaneous. Above 0 °C, TΔS > ΔH, so ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0.

explanation: With ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is positive at low T and negative at high T. At 0 °C the two terms balance, ΔG = 0, and ice and water are at equilibrium.

prompt: For NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s), the section gives ΔS = −0.285 kJ/K. Why is the entropy change negative?

choices.text: Two gases combine into one solid
The reaction gives off heat
choices.why: Heat given off shows up in ΔH = −176.2 kJ, not in the sign of the system's ΔS. ΔS < 0 because two moles of gas become one mole of solid.

choices.text: The reaction runs at constant pressure
choices.why: Constant pressure does not fix the sign of ΔS. ΔS < 0 because two moles of gas turn into one mole of an ordered solid.

choices.text: The product has more moles than the reactants
choices.why: It is the other way round: 2 mol of gas give 1 mol of solid. Fewer, more ordered particles mean lower entropy.

explanation: Two moles of gas, whose molecules move freely, become one mole of an ordered solid. That large loss of freedom makes ΔS = −0.285 kJ/K.

prompt: At 298 K, ΔG for NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s) is strongly negative. What does the section conclude?

choices.text: It runs until the limiting reagent is used up
It does not occur until it is heated above 618 K
choices.why: Above about 618 K, ΔG turns positive and the reaction runs backward. At 298 K, ΔG < 0, so it proceeds forward.

choices.text: It is already at equilibrium at 298 K
choices.why: Equilibrium would need ΔG = 0. With ΔG = −91.3 kJ, the reaction proceeds strongly forward.

choices.text: NH4Cl decomposes into NH3 and HCl
choices.why: That is what happens above about 618 K, where ΔG > 0. At 298 K, ΔG < 0, so NH4Cl forms from the gases.

explanation: ΔG = −91.3 kJ at 298 K, so the reaction proceeds toward NH4Cl(s). The section says it runs until whichever gas is the limiting reagent is used up.

prompt: Heated well above room temperature, ΔG for NH3(g) + HCl(g) ⇌ NH4Cl(s) becomes positive. What happens to solid NH4Cl then?

choices.text: It decomposes into NH3 and HCl gases
It melts but stays as NH4Cl
choices.why: Melting is not what ΔG > 0 describes here. The reverse reaction becomes spontaneous, so the salt splits into the base NH3 and the acid HCl.

choices.text: It goes on forming from the gases
choices.why: Forming NH4Cl needs ΔG < 0, which holds only below about 618 K. Above it, the reverse reaction is spontaneous.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since ΔG > 0 means no reaction
choices.why: ΔG > 0 means the forward reaction is not spontaneous, but then the reverse one is. NH4Cl decomposes into NH3 and HCl.

explanation: Above about 618 K, ΔG for forming NH4Cl is positive, so the reverse reaction, NH4Cl(s) → NH3(g) + HCl(g), has ΔG < 0. The salt decomposes into the two gases, the base and the acid.

prompt: The section estimates the temperature at which ΔG for forming NH4Cl(s) turns positive. Which assumption does this estimate rest on?

choices.text: ΔH and ΔS do not change with temperature
The pressure rises as the temperature rises
choices.why: The pressure is held at 1 bar, which is what makes ΔG the right test. The estimate assumes ΔH and ΔS keep their 298 K values.

choices.text: ΔG keeps its 298 K value of −91.3 kJ
choices.why: If ΔG stayed at −91.3 kJ, it would never change sign. ΔG changes with T through −TΔS; the assumption is that ΔH and ΔS stay fixed.

choices.text: NH3 and HCl react fully at any temperature
choices.why: The point of the estimate is that the reaction reverses at high temperature. It assumes only that ΔH and ΔS keep their 298 K values.

explanation: Setting ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = 0 with the 298 K values gives T = ΔH/ΔS ≈ 618 K. The section notes this assumes ΔH and ΔS stay the same, which is almost but not completely true.

prompt: According to the section, what does ΔG stand for in a process at constant T and P?

choices.text: The maximum non-P–V work it can perform
The maximum P–V work it can perform
choices.why: Volume work is exactly what ΔG leaves out, or corrects for. ΔG is the maximum work other than P–V work, such as electrical work.

choices.text: The heat it gives off to the surroundings
choices.why: The heat given off at constant pressure is −ΔH, not ΔG. ΔG is the maximal non-P–V work the process can perform.

choices.text: The total work, including P–V work
choices.why: At constant P the system may do volume work, but ΔG corrects for it. What remains is the maximal non-P–V work.

explanation: ΔG is the maximal reversible, isobaric, isothermal non-P–V work that a spontaneous change can perform. Any volume work done at constant P is subtracted out, or corrected for.

prompt: Which is an example of the non-P–V work that ΔG measures?

choices.text: Electrical work done by a cell
A gas pushing back the atmosphere
choices.why: That is volume work, which ΔG leaves out. Electrical work, such as driving a current, is non-P–V work.

choices.text: Heat flowing to the surroundings
choices.why: Heat is not work. Non-P–V work means work other than expansion or compression, such as electrical work.

choices.text: A piston compressing a gas
choices.why: Compressing a gas is P–V work. ΔG measures other work, such as electrical work.

explanation: Non-P–V work is any work other than expansion or compression, for example electrical or elastic work. ΔG gives the most of such work a process can do at constant T and P.

prompt: The section writes dG = δw_rev − S dT + V dP + P dV. Which two terms drop out at constant T and P?

choices.text: −S dT and V dP
δw_rev and P dV
choices.why: These two remain; together they give the useful work. −S dT and V dP vanish because dT = 0 and dP = 0.

choices.text: V dP and P dV
choices.why: P dV is not zero, since the volume can change at constant P. The terms that vanish are −S dT and V dP.

choices.text: −S dT and P dV
choices.why: P dV survives; it is minus the volume work, which the section subtracts. V dP vanishes along with −S dT, since dP = 0.

explanation: At constant T, dT = 0, so −S dT vanishes; at constant P, dP = 0, so V dP vanishes. What remains, δw_rev + P dV, is the reversible work minus the volume work: the other useful work.

prompt: Which two variables are the natural variables of the Gibbs energy G?

choices.text: Pressure P and temperature T
Volume V and temperature T
choices.why: In dG = V dP − S dT, V is a coefficient; the changes are dP and dT. So G's natural variables are P and T.

choices.text: Entropy S and pressure P
choices.why: S is the coefficient of dT in dG = V dP − S dT, not a variable that changes. The natural variables are P and T.

choices.text: Entropy S and volume V
choices.why: S and V are the coefficients in dG = V dP − S dT. The differentials are dP and dT, so G depends naturally on P and T.

explanation: Since dG = V dP − S dT, G changes naturally with P and T. These are the variables most laboratory experiments control.

prompt: Why does the section call G the most useful of the four functions U, H, A and G?

choices.text: Its natural variables, P and T, are what labs control
It is the only one of the four that is a state function
choices.why: U, H, A and G are all state functions. G stands out because its natural variables, P and T, are those of most lab experiments.

choices.text: Its natural variables are V and T, as in sealed vessels
choices.why: V and T are the natural variables of A. G's natural variables are P and T, which most lab experiments control.

choices.text: It does not depend on the temperature
choices.why: G does depend on T: dG = V dP − S dT. What makes G useful is that P and T, its natural variables, are what experiments control.

explanation: The natural variables of G are P and T, the conditions of most laboratory experiments. So dG ≤ 0 at constant T and P is the spontaneity test chemists use most.

prompt: For NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s) at 298 K and 1 bar, ΔH = −176.2 kJ and ΔS = −285 J/K. Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, what is ΔG, in kJ, including its sign? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: TΔS = (298 K)(−0.285 kJ/K) = −84.9 kJ, so ΔG = −176.2 kJ − (−84.9 kJ) = −91.3 kJ. Converting ΔS to kJ/K first keeps the units consistent, and ΔG < 0 means the salt forms.

prompt: For NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s), ΔH = −176.2 kJ and ΔS = −0.285 kJ/K. Taking both as constant, ΔG = 0 at T = ΔH/ΔS. Above what temperature does ΔG become positive, in K? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: T = (−176.2 kJ)/(−0.285 kJ/K) = 618.2 K. Below this temperature ΔG < 0 and NH4Cl forms; above it ΔG > 0 and the salt decomposes into NH3 and HCl.

prompt: For melting 1 mol of ice, take ΔH = +6.01 kJ and ΔS = +22.0 J/K, both constant. Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, what is ΔG for melting at 283 K, in J, including its sign?
explanation: TΔS = (283 K)(22.0 J/K) = 6226 J, so ΔG = 6010 J − 6226 J = −216 J. ΔG < 0, so at 10 °C ice melts, just as the section says it does above 0 °C.

prompt: A fuel cell runs H2(g) + ½O2(g) → H2O(ℓ) at 298 K and 1 bar, with ΔH = −285.8 kJ and ΔS = −163.3 J/K. Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, what is the most electrical (non-P–V) work the reaction can do, in kJ? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: TΔS = (298 K)(−0.1633 kJ/K) = −48.7 kJ, so ΔG = −285.8 kJ + 48.7 kJ = −237.1 kJ. At most 237.1 kJ can be drawn as electrical work, less than the 285.8 kJ of heat that burning the hydrogen would give.

prompt: A process at constant T and a constant pressure of 1.00 × 10^5 Pa has ΔA = −50.0 kJ, and its volume grows by ΔV = 0.0200 m^3. Since G = A + PV, at constant P, ΔG = ΔA + PΔV. What is ΔG, in kJ, including its sign?
explanation: PΔV = (1.00 × 10^5 Pa)(0.0200 m^3) = 2000 J = 2.00 kJ, so ΔG = −50.0 kJ + 2.00 kJ = −48.0 kJ. The two differ by PΔV, the volume work of the expansion, which ΔG leaves out.

prompt: A process has ΔH = +20.0 kJ and ΔS = −50.0 J/K. Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, what is ΔG at 400 K, in kJ, including its sign?
explanation: TΔS = (400 K)(−0.0500 kJ/K) = −20.0 kJ, so ΔG = 20.0 kJ − (−20.0 kJ) = +40.0 kJ. With ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0, both terms are positive, so ΔG > 0 at every temperature.
